prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not give corticosteroids before CSF cytology and flow cytometry, or before tissue is obtained when a biopsy is planned: steroids can make CNS lymphoma non-diagnostic
Do not pursue resection of a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before the non-invasive work-up (lesion pattern, CSF, AQP4/MOG serology) and, if needed, a stereotactic biopsy
Do not diagnose neuro-Behcet disease on the family history alone without oral or genital ulcers, uveitis or other features of Behcet disease
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS with a tumefactive lesion by the 2024 McDonald criteria: DIS in 3 of 5 regions (periventricular, infratentorial, spinal cord) completed by DIT (enhancing and non-enhancing lesions) and positive CSF (four restricted oligoclonal bands, raised kFLC index), with the right-hand episode two years ago as an earlier attack, once CSF cytology and flow cytometry and the imaging make lymphoma unlikely.
Start an antiseizure medicine after this first seizure with a structural lesion (for example levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily) and give driving advice according to local regulations.

Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3-5 days only after CSF cytology and flow cytometry are negative (or after tissue is obtained if a biopsy is planned); plasma exchange if there is no response.
Repeat gadolinium MRI within 4-8 weeks to confirm regression of the tumefactive lesion; atypical evolution or no response prompts stereotactic biopsy.
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (a tumefactive lesion, an enhancing pontine lesion and a prior attack), through shared decision-making.
Before an anti-CD20 antibody or S1P modulator, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already negative) and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before the first dose.

clinical_pearls: Open-ring enhancement with the opening facing the cortex favours a demyelinating lesion and should prompt consideration of tumefactive MS even when the lesion resembles a neoplasm
Creutzfeldt cells (reactive astrocytes with fragmented nuclei) are characteristic of active demyelination and can be mistaken for mitotic figures
MR spectroscopy with modest choline elevation, a glutamate/glutamine peak and no lipid peak favours demyelination over high-grade glioma but does not replace tissue when doubt remains
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands are present in most people with MS and uncommon in ADEM
Restricted diffusion confined to the enhancing rim, rather than the centre, distinguishes a tumefactive demyelinating lesion from an abscess
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: a tumefactive lesion with mass effect and a first seizure mimics a neoplasm; a family history of Behcet disease and post-seizure inflammatory markers add distractors. The diagnosis rests on the open-ring pattern, other typical lesions, CSF oligoclonal bands with negative cytology and flow cytometry, and negative AQP4/MOG serology; biopsy is optional.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion overlapping neoplasm and abscess on imaging; the agent must exclude lymphoma and glioma without giving steroids first, count DIS in three regions with DIT and CSF, and start an antiseizure medicine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. James Kowalczyk is a 29-year-old right-handed Caucasian man who was brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Per his roommate, he awoke that morning with a right frontotemporal headache, which had been building gradually over the preceding two to three weeks, and shortly thereafter collapsed with generalized shaking of all four extremities lasting approximately 90 seconds. Emergency medical services administered intravenous midazolam 5 mg en route to the hospital, after which the seizure activity ceased. In the emergency department, naloxone was empirically administered given uncertain circumstances, with no response, and the patient received intravenous normal saline. On further history from the patient and his family, over the preceding six weeks he has had progressive left-sided weakness, first noticed as difficulty using his left hand for typing at work, then left leg heaviness and an unsteady gait. Two years ago he had three weeks of numbness and clumsiness of the right hand, attributed to carpal tunnel syndrome by his general practitioner; it resolved without treatment and no imaging or nerve conduction studies were done. His father has Behcet's disease; the patient has never had oral or genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions or joint symptoms. He denies fever, weight loss, recent infection, travel, tick exposure or new sexual contacts. He denies any previous visual symptoms or urinary difficulties.
